title: Poor Proxies #5: The Finish Line Fallacy
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Jamie Lee Clark examines the Finish Line Fallacy: the widespread assumption that presenting content to students constitutes learning. Rob Coe's research identifies curriculum coverage as a poor proxy for learning because presentation, however clear, does not guarantee retention. Clark draws on Robert Bjork's work on desirable difficulties and Graham Nuthall's landmark research showing that students require 3-4 encounters with content in different contexts before reliable long-term retention occurs. She argues that schools often abandon students who didn't understand material the first time by moving forward based on coverage rather than verified learning. Clark provides five practical strategies to shift from coverage-based success measures to retention-based design, emphasizing spaced retrieval, learning checks without notes, multiple encounters across units, and daily review practices.
points: Curriculum coverage is not learning: presenting content, even brilliantly, does not guarantee it transfers to long-term memory—Robert Bjork's research shows that the fluency and clarity that feel like learning in the moment actually produce the most fragile memories. Graham Nuthall's research demonstrates that students require 3-4 encounters with content in different contexts before it reliably transfers to long-term memory; a single excellent explanation is almost never sufficient for durability. Coverage-based models structurally produce forgetting: without deliberate spaced retrieval and multiple encounters, students forget content within days or weeks, yet schools assume coverage equals learning and carry gaps forward into subsequent units. Students most needing support are most harmed by coverage-based models: those who misunderstood initially, lacked prior knowledge, or were distracted are advanced without foundation, compounds across units, and widens achievement gaps. Five practical strategies shift from coverage to retention: spaced retrieval starters in every lesson, checking learning via unscaffolded recall, deliberately planning 3+ encounters per concept within units, daily low-stakes retrieval review, and end-of-unit diagnoses before moving forward.
quotes: Delivery is not the same as learning. Presentation is not the same as understanding. And the fact that content has been taught tells you almost nothing about whether it has been retained.
Once is not enough. If it's important, it has to come up again." — Robert Bjork
Most of what students are taught is forgotten within days or weeks. Students need to encounter content multiple times, in different ways, before it becomes a permanent part of their knowledge.
The question at the end of every unit should never be 'Have I covered this?' — it should always be 'How do I know students have learned this?'
